newsitem.title: USA: Betty Shabazz badly burned in suspicious fire.
newsitem.headline: Betty Shabazz badly burned in suspicious fire.

text.p: Betty Shabazz, the widow of slain civil rights leader Malcolm X, is in critical condition with burns over 80 percent of her body from a fire that authorities described as suspicious, police said on Sunday.
Shabazz was found at 1:40 a.m. EDT (0540 GMT) in her posh co-op apartment in Westchester County, New York, and rushed to the burn unit at Jacobi Hospital in the New York borough of the Bronx.
William Rinaldi, a Yonkers, New York, detective said she was listed in critical condition with third-degree burns.
"This is an on-going investigation," Rinaldi said. "The fire is being labeled suspicious at this time."
Police would not comment on how the fire started or who may have set the blaze. They said there was little fire damage to the apartment.

Police added that a male youth who is a relative of Shabazz and who originally had been reported missing from the apartment had been located. But they would neither identify the relative nor say whether he was a suspect.

The apartment in which Shabazz was found is near the Westchester community of Bronxville, about 20 miles (32 km) north of Manhattan. It is a three-bedroom unit on the top floor of a six-floor building.

A hospital spokesman confirmed that Shabazz was in critical condition but said the family requested that no other details be provided. Shabazz heads the Office of Institutional Advancement at Medgar Evers College in Brooklyn, N.Y.

Malcolm X, a civil rights leader who promoted black pride, was gunned down in 1965 while giving a speech at the Audubon Theatre in Manhattan. The Shabazz family had long said they believed controversial Nation of Islam leader Louis Farrakhan, Malcolm X's bitter enemy before his assassination, played a role in the shooting.
Police did not say whether Farrakhan or the Nation of Islam is suspected in the blaze.
Qubilah Bahiyah Shabazz, Malcolm X's daughter, had been indicted in January 1995 on charges she tried to hire a man to kill Farrakhan.
In a deal with prosecutors in 1995, Qubilah Shabazz accepted responsibility for her role in the murder-for-hire plot and agreed to seek psychiatric help during probation.
On May 1, 1997, federal prosecutors dismissed the daughter's indictment after they said she had successfully completed a two-year probationary period.

According to the original federal indictment of Qubilah Shabazz, she teamed up with a childhood friend to kill Farrakhan because she believed him responsible for her father's death and worried he was also planning to kill her mother.
Malcolm X had been Farrakhan's spiritual mentor and for many years the right-hand man and heir apparent to Elijah Muhammad, head of the Nation of Islam.

Farrakhan was never indicted or formally implicated in his mentor's death. But he publicly threatened Malcolm in the months before the murder and allegations were made at the time that he was involved in planning the crime.
In 1995 Shabazz and Farrakhan met at the Apollo Theatre on 125th Street in the Harlem section of Manhattan to patch up their rift in a much-publicised meeting.

At the reconciliation, attended by more than 1,400 of Harlem's most prominent politicians and civic leaders, Farrakhan turned to Betty Shabazz as she sat on the stage next to him, and asked for her forgiveness.
Members of the Nation of Islam were involved in Malcolm's assassination, acknowledged Farrakhan. "We cannot deny our part," he said.
Farrakhan denied any personal involvment in the killing himself, but he conceded that his "zeal" and "love" for Elijah Muhammad had been "manipulated" and he apologised for the "hurt and offence."
Farrakhan was harshly critical of authorities for charging Quibilah Shabazz in the case.
